analysis.one_liner: Bars insurers from taking a share of an injury settlement until the insured is fully paid.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, leaving insurers free to recover payments from injury victims before the victims are fully compensated.
analysis.plain_summary: When an insurance company pays for someone's injuries and that person later wins money from the party at fault, many policies let the insurer recoup its payment first. This bill would flip that order: no insurer could claim reimbursement until the injured person had been made whole and the insurer had actually paid the claim. It was introduced in the House in 2000 and referred to the Commerce Committee, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Injured people who carry health, auto, or disability insurance. If they recover damages from the person who hurt them, they would keep enough of that recovery to cover all their losses before the insurer takes any of it. The CRS summary describes the rule the bill would impose: no insurer could exercise a subrogation or reimbursement right until the insured was fully compensated for the injuries and the insurer had made payment [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill would stop insurers from using subrogation or reimbursement clauses to take back their payments out of an injury settlement before the injured person has been made whole, so a victim who is still out-of-pocket keeps their recovery instead of watching the insurer collect first [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health, auto, and casualty insurers, which would lose the ability to recoup claim payments from injury victims' settlements until those victims were fully compensated [S2] [S3]. Insurers would argue that this shifts some costs back into premiums for all policyholders; the bill text and summary do not include any offsetting mechanism [S3].

drawbacks.text: Insurers use subrogation to recover double recoveries and keep premiums lower; barring collection until the insured is fully made whole would raise their costs, and those costs would likely be passed back to policyholders through higher premiums. The bill contains no provision addressing premium impacts [S3].

The bill would invite disputes over what 'fully compensated' means — future medical costs, pain and suffering, and attorney fees are all hard to quantify — which could slow settlements and increase litigation between policyholders and insurers [S3].

It was a one-page, single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors and no committee action, so there was never a hearing record weighing its costs and benefits; the proposed mechanism also rests only on an insurer being 'engaged in interstate commerce', a hook whose reach for purely local policies is untested [S1] [S4] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and concrete: an injury victim who wins a settlement would keep it until whole, rather than paying the insurer back first. But the bill is a single sentence with no definitions, no premium safeguard, and no testing of how 'fully compensated' would be determined in practice, so its costs (premium pressure, settlement disputes) are unaddressed on the face of the text. As drafted it would have needed committee refinement before it could responsibly become law; as introduced, it died without that ever happening [S2] [S3] [S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John J. Duncan Jr. introduced the bill on March 29, 2000, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].

On April 6, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials, where no further action was recorded; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5] [S1].
No other member cosponsored the bill at any point [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health, auto, and casualty insurers came out ahead: they kept their existing right to recover claim payments from injury victims' settlements before those victims are fully compensated. For injured policyholders, nothing changed.

for.name: Rep. John J. Duncan Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 29, 2000; it was his only action — the bill attracted no cosponsors

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there

against.name: Health and casualty insurers
against.role: Industry whose reimbursement rights the bill would have restricted
against.what_they_did: Industry opposition to limits on subrogation and reimbursement rights is well documented in state and federal insurance debates

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no record of partisan alignment exists [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have stripped insurers of their ability to recoup claim payments from a policyholder's injury settlement until the policyholder was made whole. Their interest in the bill ran against the injured policyholders it would protect, because what insurers recover in subrogation is money those victims would otherwise keep [S2] [S3].
